knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
library(uncertR)
Overview

uncertR provides bootstrap-based estimates of prediction uncertainty for regression models. The package uses out-of-bag (OOB) predictions from bootstrap models to quantify how much predictions vary across bootstrap replicates.

This vignette demonstrates the basic workflow using a small simulated gene-expression dataset. The example is intentionally small so that it runs quickly and does not require a large external dataset.

Simulating gene-expression and drug-response data

We first create a gene-expression matrix with genes as rows and samples as columns. We then simulate a drug-response phenotype that depends on several genes.

set.seed(42)

n_genes <- 100
n_samples <- 80

expr <- matrix(
  rnorm(n_genes * n_samples),
  nrow = n_genes,
  ncol = n_samples,
  dimnames = list(
    paste0("Gene", seq_len(n_genes)),
    paste0("Sample", seq_len(n_samples))
  )
)

y <- 2 * expr[1, ] -
  1.5 * expr[2, ] +
  0.8 * expr[3, ] +
  rnorm(n_samples, sd = 1)

dim(expr)
length(y)
Bootstrap prediction uncertainty

boot_uncertainty() fits an ensemble of bootstrap models and generates out-of-bag predictions for each sample. An observation is out-of-bag for a bootstrap replicate when that observation was not selected in the bootstrap training sample.

For this example, we use 40 bootstrap replicates to keep computation relatively short.

fit <- boot_uncertainty(
  expr = expr,
  y = y,
  B = 40,
  seed = 42
)

fit

The OOB prediction matrix contains one column for each bootstrap replicate. Samples that were included in a particular bootstrap training set have an NA for that replicate.

dim(fit$oob)
head(fit$oob[, 1:5])
Calculating uncertainty scores

uncertainty_score() summarizes the variability of the OOB predictions for each sample. Three measures are available: standard deviation ("sd"), interquartile range ("iqr"), and confidence-interval width ("ci_width").

unc_sd <- uncertainty_score(
  fit,
  metric = "sd",
  min_oob = 5
)

head(unc_sd$scores)

The same bootstrap predictions can be summarized using the other metrics:

unc_iqr <- uncertainty_score(
  fit,
  metric = "iqr",
  min_oob = 5
)

unc_ci <- uncertainty_score(
  fit,
  metric = "ci_width",
  min_oob = 5
)

head(unc_iqr$scores)
head(unc_ci$scores)

Higher uncertainty scores indicate greater variation among the OOB predictions for a sample.

Relating uncertainty to prediction error

Prediction uncertainty and prediction error are distinct quantities. uncertainty_score() measures the dispersion of bootstrap predictions, while validate_uncertainty() can be used to examine whether estimated uncertainty is associated with prediction error.

validation <- validate_uncertainty(unc_sd)

validation
Investigating potential drivers of uncertainty

uncertainty_drivers() can be used to examine whether sample-level covariates are associated with estimated uncertainty.

Here, we create two example covariates and use the uncertainty estimates generated above.

set.seed(42)

covariates <- data.frame(
  purity = runif(n_samples),
  technical_factor = rnorm(n_samples),
  row.names = rownames(unc_sd$scores)
)

drivers <- uncertainty_drivers(
  unc_sd,
  covariates,
  n_perm = 100,
  seed = 42
)

drivers$table
Additional utility functions

uncertR also provides utilities for working with covariates.

For example, collapse_rare_levels() combines categorical levels with fewer than a specified number of observations into "Other".

tissue <- c(
  rep("Tissue_A", 30),
  rep("Tissue_B", 30),
  rep("Rare", 5),
  rep("Rare_2", 5)
)

collapse_rare_levels(tissue, min_n = 10)

For compositional data such as cell-type fractions, clr_transform() applies a centered log-ratio transformation.

fractions <- matrix(
  c(
    0.2, 0.3, 0.5,
    0.1, 0.1, 0.8
  ),
  nrow = 2,
  byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(
    paste0("Sample", 1:2),
    c("CellTypeA", "CellTypeB", "CellTypeC")
  )
)

clr_transform(fractions)
Summary

A basic uncertR workflow is:

Provide a gene-expression matrix and response variable.
Generate bootstrap models and OOB predictions with boot_uncertainty().
Summarize prediction uncertainty with uncertainty_score().
Examine the relationship between uncertainty and prediction error with validate_uncertainty().
Investigate potential biological or technical drivers with uncertainty_drivers().

The vignette uses simulated data so that it remains lightweight, reproducible, and suitable for automated package checks without requiring a large external dataset.
